paragraph:
As Bharata was desolately recollecting his dream, the messengers from Ayodhya arrived. Presenting themselves to Bharata, they conveyed Vasishta's message. "Vasishta offers you his salutations and those of the ministers. He wishes your immediate return to Ayodhya, as an urgent matter requires your attention." Bharata enquired of the welfare of Dastaratha, Rama and Lakshmana. "How fares noble mother Kausalya?" Bharata wanted to know, "and what of Sumitra an equally virtuous mother and that irascible, forceful and selfish lady, my mother, in awe of her own intelligence and virtue, which sets her apart".

The messengers assured Bharata that all was well and that they should think of journeying back to Ayodhya. The king of Kekaya tenderly kissed Bharata on his brow blessed him and bade him an affectionate farewell. He also bestowed on his grandson a part of all that he possessed. He gave well-bred elephants, thoroughbred dogs, raised with care in the palace which were as ferocious as tigers. Gold nuggets, woolens, fine clothes, antelope skins along with sixteen thousand horses were added to Bharata's entourage, as also the elephants Airavata and Indrasra, which were presented by Yudhajit. Distinguished counselors were to accompany Bharata, as a mark of respect and honor. Nothing of this pomp or the generous display of his grand father's love for him cheered Bharata nor impressed him, as he was impatient to be on his way. An inexplicable gloom that had settled on him refused to be dispelled.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Bharata, already disturbed by ominous dreams, receives an urgent but vague summons to Ayodhya. He quizzes the messengers about his family, showing keen perception in his critical description of his own mother, Kaikeyi. Despite being reassured that all is well and receiving magnificent parting gifts, Bharata is overwhelmed by a persistent and inexplicable sense of gloom, unable to find any joy or comfort.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage highlights the power of intuition and premonition, as Bharata's inner gloom correctly senses a tragedy that verbal assurances cannot mask. It builds intense dramatic irony, as the audience is aware of the truth that Bharata is not. It also reveals Bharata's righteous character through his concern for all family members and establishes his detachment from material wealth, which holds no power over his profound inner turmoil.
Outcome/Resolution: Bharata receives the message and agrees to return to Ayodhya immediately. Although the messengers falsely assure him of his family's welfare, and his grandfather lavishes him with honors and immense wealth, his deep sense of foreboding is not relieved. Impatient and uncheered by the pomp, he begins his journey back, enveloped in a gloom he cannot understand.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.anxiety: Intuitive dread, Unshakable despondency, Foreboding sadness

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Haunted by 'Ashubha Nimitta' (inauspicious omens) from his dream, Bharata is immersed in 'Chinta' (anxiety). The messengers from Ayodhya convey 'Mithya' (falsehood), a deception that fails to pierce his intuitive gloom. Bharata's deep 'Bandhu Sneha' (familial affection) is evident in his specific inquiries, and he displays a profound 'Vairagya' (detachment) from the lavish gifts, as his inner turmoil renders material wealth meaningless while he rushes to face the 'Karma' unfolding in Ayodhya.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Bharata exhibits strong premonitory anxiety and a persistent depressive mood ('desolately,' 'inexplicable gloom'), which are not alleviated by external factors like gifts or verbal reassurances. This highlights the power of intuition over explicit information. The messengers engage in information control and deception, creating intense dramatic irony. Bharata's critical assessment of his mother reveals his astute perception of personality dynamics. His complete indifference to the magnificent gifts underscores how profound inner turmoil can negate the pleasure-giving capacity of external rewards.
